questions.statement: Which option best states the main idea of the whole text?
questions.context: A text describes how a fishing village in a dry region stores rainwater, treats it and rations it during the dry months.

options.text: The text explains how a coastal community manages its water supply.
options.feedback: Correct! This option covers the whole text without adding anything it does not contain.

options.text: The text lists the names of the wells dug in the region.
options.feedback: The names of the wells are only a detail inside one section of the text.

options.text: The text compares two families who live by the sea.
options.feedback: The two families appear in a single paragraph and are not the subject of the whole text.

options.text: The text describes a storm that damaged a village in 1998.
options.feedback: The storm is one episode, and the text uses it only to introduce the wider problem.

questions.explanation:
The main idea is the point the whole text serves. An option that covers every paragraph without adding material is the one that answers the question.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the best title for the text?
questions.context: The same text explains water collection, filtration and community rules in a dry region.

options.text: A Village Lost in a Storm
options.feedback: The storm is one event in one paragraph and cannot represent the whole text.

options.text: Saving Water in a Dry Region
options.feedback: Correct! The title covers the topic of the whole text in a few words.

options.text: The Names of Old Wells
options.feedback: The names of the wells are a detail that appears briefly.

options.text: Two Families of the Coast
options.feedback: The two families are a short episode and do not represent the subject of the text.

questions.explanation:
A good title is broad enough to include every paragraph and narrow enough not to include material the text does not treat.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which paragraph would you read first to find out what the main problem is?
questions.context: A six-paragraph text moves from the problem to the responses and ends with general comments.

options.text: The last paragraph, which gives a list of figures.
options.feedback: The last paragraph gives figures, which are details rather than the statement of the problem.

options.text: The fourth paragraph, which describes a family.
options.feedback: The fourth paragraph describes a family, which is an episode and not the framing of the text.

options.text: The first paragraph, which presents the shortage.
options.feedback: Correct! The first paragraph presents the shortage, which is the problem the rest of the text addresses.

options.text: The sixth paragraph, which mentions an old custom.
options.feedback: The sixth paragraph mentions a custom, which is a closing detail.

questions.explanation:
Texts normally introduce their main problem at the beginning. Reading the opening paragraph is the fastest way to identify the subject.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The text says the water committee was created in 1996. What does this detail mainly tell the reader?
questions.context: A text about water management states that the local committee was set up some years before the worst drought.

options.text: That the committee has no members today.
options.feedback: The text does not say that the committee has no members.

options.text: That the region has no wells at all.
options.feedback: The text says the opposite, since the wells are the source of the system.

options.text: That the community rejected the idea of saving water.
options.feedback: The text describes the opposite, since the committee exists precisely to save water.

options.text: That the solution is older than the crisis it responds to.
options.feedback: Correct! The date places the committee before the drought, so the response predates the crisis it solves.

questions.explanation:
A detail matters most when it shows the relationship between two facts stated elsewhere in the text. The date places the committee before the drought.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which of these is NOT an argument the text uses?
questions.context: A text argues for water saving, better storage and clear rules for sharing a limited supply.

options.text: That tourism should be limited in the region.
options.feedback: Correct! The text never argues about tourism, so that argument does not appear in it.

options.text: That every drop must be counted.
options.feedback: Counting every drop is one of the recommendations the text makes.

options.text: That rules are needed to share the supply.
options.feedback: Clear rules for sharing the supply are a central proposal of the text.

options.text: That rainwater storage must be improved.
options.feedback: Improving rainwater storage is described as the practical solution.

questions.explanation:
To find what the text does not use, check each option against the arguments it does develop. Tourism is never mentioned as a problem.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How would you summarise the text in one sentence?
questions.context: A text presents a community response to a water shortage through storage, filtration and local rules.

options.text: Several paragraphs describe the weather of a coastal plain.
options.feedback: The weather is not the subject of the text and appears only as background.

options.text: A dry region solved a water shortage by combining storage, filtration and community rules.
options.feedback: Correct! This summary keeps the problem, the three measures and the result, and omits the illustrations.

options.text: The text lists the different wells dug since 1996.
options.feedback: The wells are listed as a detail, not as the substance of the text.

options.text: Two neighbouring villages argued about how to share a well.
options.feedback: The disagreement between two villages is a short episode, not the topic.

questions.explanation:
A summary keeps the topic, the main actions and the outcome, and leaves out the illustrations and the small details.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the function of the second paragraph of the text?
questions.context: The first paragraph presents the shortage, the second the filtration process and the last the rules.

options.text: It concludes the whole argument with a final recommendation.
options.feedback: The conclusion is in the last paragraph, not in the second.

options.text: It introduces the problem the text is about.
options.feedback: The introduction of the problem is in the first paragraph.

options.text: It explains how the collected water is treated before it is used.
options.feedback: Correct! The second paragraph develops the text by explaining how the water is treated.

options.text: It presents a personal opinion of the author.
options.feedback: The author reports a community process and does not give a personal opinion.

questions.explanation:
Paragraph function is read from its place in the structure: introduction, development, examples and conclusion each have their own job.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement best describes the general idea of the last paragraph?
questions.context: A text about water management closes by explaining what makes the community system sustainable.

options.text: Most families keep the water for their own use.
options.feedback: The text says the opposite, since hoarding water would defeat the shared system.

options.text: The wells have dried up completely.
options.feedback: The text describes wells that still work, not wells that have dried up.

options.text: The region has more water than it did in the past.
options.feedback: The region is described as having less water than before, not more.

options.text: The rules work only if the whole community follows them.
options.feedback: Correct! The closing paragraph generalises by stating the condition on which the system works.

questions.explanation:
A concluding paragraph usually generalises from the details. The condition for success is the idea it leaves the reader with.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The text mentions a public meeting. Why is it included?
questions.context: A text describes a public meeting at which residents agreed on new rules for the water supply.

options.text: To show how a decision was agreed by the community.
options.feedback: Correct! The meeting is included to show that the rules were agreed by the people who follow them.

options.text: To prove that the water committee was a failure.
options.feedback: The text presents the meeting as a success, not as a failure.

options.text: To describe the personal life of a committee member.
options.feedback: Nothing about a member's personal life is described there.

options.text: To fill the paragraph with an unrelated anecdote.
options.feedback: The anecdote is directly related to the main argument, so it is not filler.

questions.explanation:
Details in a text are included for a reason. An example of a meeting shows how the rules were accepted, which supports the main argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which detail is least relevant to the main idea of the text?
questions.context: A text on water management mixes the core argument with one short reference to a school visit.

options.text: The need to store rainwater.
options.feedback: Storing rainwater is one of the three measures the text describes.

options.text: The name of the school that visited the wells.
options.feedback: Correct! The school visit is a passing mention and removing it would leave the argument intact.

options.text: The shortage of water in the dry months.
options.feedback: The shortage is the problem the whole text exists to address.

options.text: The rules for sharing the supply.
options.feedback: The rules for sharing the supply are the central recommendation.

questions.explanation:
A detail is relevant when it supports the main idea. The school visit is a passing mention that could be removed without changing the argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the text want the reader to remember at the end?
questions.context: A text argues that a water crisis was addressed through both technical measures and local agreements.

options.text: That wells are more useful than rainfall.
options.feedback: The text does not rank wells above rainfall but treats both as parts of the system.

options.text: That one family solved the problem alone.
options.feedback: No single family is presented as having solved the problem.

options.text: That saving water depends on both engineering and community agreement.
options.feedback: Correct! The conclusion reinforces that the solution combined physical works with community agreement.

options.text: That the region has no need for new rules.
options.feedback: The text argues for exactly such new rules.

questions.explanation:
The message a text wants remembered is the one its conclusion reinforces and the whole text has been building towards.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which word or phrase in the text best shows that the situation was serious?
questions.context: A text about a water shortage uses several expressions to describe how little water families had left.

options.text: A pleasant surprise
options.feedback: A pleasant surprise contradicts the serious tone of the text.

options.text: A minor inconvenience
options.feedback: A minor inconvenience understates a shortage that closed public buildings.

options.text: An unexpected holiday
options.feedback: An unexpected holiday has no connection to the water problem.

options.text: Only a few hours of water
options.feedback: Correct! A quantified expression such as 'only a few hours' shows the severity of the shortage.

questions.explanation:
Lexical markers of severity are quantified expressions, and they carry the gravity of the situation better than a general opinion.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: How does the text organise its information?
questions.context: A text on water management opens with the shortage, develops the solutions and closes with a condition.

options.text: By moving from the problem to the measures and ending with their condition of success.
options.feedback: Correct! The text follows the standard order of problem, measures and conclusion.

options.text: By listing the wells in the order in which they were dug.
options.feedback: The wells appear as examples inside the text, not as its organisational principle.

options.text: By presenting three unrelated anecdotes in order.
options.feedback: The paragraphs are connected and build one argument, so they are not unrelated.

options.text: By comparing the region with two other countries.
options.feedback: The text stays within the region and does not compare it with other countries.

questions.explanation:
Organisation is recognised by the order of the paragraphs: problem, development, examples and conclusion form a clear progression.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option expresses an idea that the text supports with evidence?
questions.context: A text presents technical measures together with changes in daily habits inside the home.

options.text: That the problem can be solved without any change in behaviour.
options.feedback: The text argues the opposite, since behaviour change is part of the solution.

options.text: That simple household changes also reduce the pressure on the supply.
options.feedback: Correct! The text gives specific household measures, so this idea is supported with evidence.

options.text: That only large companies are responsible for the shortage.
options.feedback: The text focuses on households and the local committee, not on companies.

options.text: That the wells produce more water than they used to.
options.feedback: The text describes a decline in the yield of the wells, not an increase.

questions.explanation:
An idea supported with evidence is one the text develops with figures, examples or named measures. Claims left without support cannot be traced back.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The text says the committee meets 'twice a month'. What does this expression do in the text?
questions.context: A text mentions a fixed meeting schedule for a local water committee as evidence of how the rules are applied.

options.text: It proves that the committee is inactive most of the time.
options.feedback: Meeting twice a month is a normal working rhythm, not inactivity.

options.text: It indicates that nobody attends the meetings.
options.feedback: The text says nothing about attendance at those meetings.

options.text: It shows the rules are checked regularly, not only once.
options.feedback: Correct! A regular schedule shows that the rules are applied continuously, not as a single decision.

options.text: It suggests the committee has run out of funds.
options.feedback: Nothing in the sentence concerns the funds of the committee.

questions.explanation:
Frequency expressions in a text are rarely decorative. Here the schedule shows the rules have a permanent mechanism behind them.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which question would the reader be least able to answer after reading the text?
questions.context: A text about water management explains the causes of the shortage and the local response to it.

options.text: Why the region suffers from a water shortage.
options.feedback: The causes of the shortage are explained in the opening of the text.

options.text: How the community stores and treats water.
options.feedback: The storage and treatment of water are described in the middle sections.

options.text: What rules the community agreed to follow.
options.feedback: The agreed rules are set out in the later paragraphs.

options.text: How much a new roof costs in the capital.
options.feedback: Correct! The text says nothing about the price of roofs, so that question remains unanswered.

questions.explanation:
A reader can only answer what the text actually covers. Questions about unrelated costs are left unanswered by design.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence would not belong in this text?
questions.context: A text treats water management in a dry region, with examples of tanks, rules and meetings.

options.text: There are twenty-four different species of parrot in the region.
options.feedback: Correct! The number of parrot species has no connection to water management and does not belong.

options.text: The committee meets twice a month to review the supply.
options.feedback: The meeting schedule is part of the account of how the rules are applied.

options.text: Storage tanks were built on the roofs of the oldest houses.
options.feedback: The storage tanks are one of the measures the text describes.

options.text: The rules were accepted after a public meeting in the village.
options.feedback: The public meeting is the example that shows how the rules were agreed.

questions.explanation:
A sentence belongs when it supports the subject of the text. A fact about birds has no link to the water supply.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the attitude of the writer towards the community rules?
questions.context: A text treats the community agreements as the decisive part of a water management programme.

options.text: Hostile, because the text criticises the people who break them.
options.feedback: The text does not criticise the community, and the writer's tone is approving.

options.text: Positive, because the text presents them as the element that makes the works succeed.
options.feedback: Correct! The writer supports the rules, since the text closes by presenting them as the decisive element.

options.text: Indifferent, because the writer never mentions them.
options.feedback: The rules occupy a central part of the text, so they are not ignored.

options.text: Doubtful, because the text says they failed completely.
options.feedback: The text presents the programme as working, not as a complete failure.

questions.explanation:
Attitude is inferred from the choices the writer makes: what is emphasised, approved or criticised. A text that ends by praising an element is positive towards it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which option would make the best concluding sentence for a text like this one?
questions.context: A text explains a community programme and is expected to end by generalising its lesson.

options.text: The wells are located near the river that feeds them.
options.feedback: The location of the wells is a fact that belongs in the body of the text.

options.text: The committee was created in the year 1996.
options.feedback: The date of the committee is a piece of information, not a conclusion.

options.text: The programme will last only if the agreements are kept by everyone.
options.feedback: Correct! This sentence generalises the lesson of the text rather than adding a new detail.

options.text: Rainfall in the region has decreased over the last decade.
options.feedback: The decrease in rainfall belongs in the section on the causes.

questions.explanation:
A conclusion generalises, it does not introduce a new fact. The first option takes the details of the text and draws the general lesson from them.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which of the following best captures the purpose of the whole text?
questions.context: A text presents a community response to a water shortage and argues that the approach works.

options.text: To entertain the reader with an account of a long journey.
options.feedback: There is no narrative journey to entertain the reader with.

options.text: To list the personal details of several committee members.
options.feedback: No personal details of members are given.

options.text: To persuade readers to visit the region as tourists.
options.feedback: The text never addresses tourism and does not invite a visit.

options.text: To explain and justify a local response to an environmental problem.
options.feedback: Correct! The text explains a response and defends it, which is an informational and persuasive purpose.

questions.explanation:
Purpose is the action the text performs on the reader. Explaining and justifying an answer to a problem is a purpose, and the others belong to other genres.
---
questions.subject: ingles
